newsitem.title: CHILE: IDB raises Latin American 1997 growth forecast.
newsitem.headline: IDB raises Latin American 1997 growth forecast.

text.p: The Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) has raised its forecast of Latin America's economic growth this year to 4.5-five percent from four percent, said president Enrique Iglesias.

"We started at four percent...but it (growth) is going to be between 4.5 and five percent," Iglesias told reporters after a meeting with Chilean Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat. "This is an important advance with respect to last year and much better compared with 1995, when we had a sharp fall due to the tequila effect," said Iglesias referring to financial turmoil following Mexico's late 1994 devaluation of the peso.
The main reason for the rise in the IDB's forecast was stronger-than-expected growth in Mexico and Argentina.
"The larger economies are behaving better than we expected, that's the only reason (for the increase)," said Iglesias.
Argentina is likely to grow at least five percent this year, which is much higher than analysts had been anticipating at the start of 1997. Mexico is also likely to expand close to five percent.
"They (the Mexicans) are working around four percent, but I think it will be close to five percent," said Iglesias.

Despite the revival of the region's economies, much still has to be done before many countries can match growth seen in Chile whose economy has expanded at least seven percent annually in recent years.
"We have to say that we are not satisfied with the rythym of growth, which should come close to level seen in Chile," he said.
Iglesias said key elements for growth included boosting domestic savings and opening the region's economies to foreign trade and investment.
